reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile carries no real tension: a .412 xwOBA and 54.2% hard-hit rate at the plate, paired with a 2.71 xERA and 98.1 mph fastball on the mound, is simply the most complete two-way profile the sport has produced. The one honest wrinkle is a 30.4% whiff rate as a hitter, which keeps him off the truly elite contact tiers and explains why the projection lands at .286 rather than something more exotic. What the walk rate does, at 14.3%, is prop up a .394 OBP even when pitchers beat him with spin, so the damage floor stays high regardless. If the pitching side returns cleanly from the Tommy John recovery and the bat stays this loud, a .942 OPS and 37 home runs across 689 projected plate appearances is the floor, not the ceiling.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: A 94.3 mph average exit velocity ranks in the 99th percentile, and when you pair that with a 14.8% barrel rate and 53.1% hard-hit rate, the .370 xwOBA stops looking like noise and starts looking like a floor. The whole profile is a blunt instrument built around elite contact quality, and the projection's .271/.350/.489 line across 633 PA reflects that the bat plays even before you add 32 projected stolen bases. The catch is the 27.1% strikeout rate, which keeps that xBA of .277 from fully translating to the surface — if he can't get that whiff rate below its current 28.3%, some of that raw power will keep evaporating against quality spin. But at 24, with this kind of athleticism and a 10.6% walk rate already suggesting he's not completely lost at the plate, you're looking at a legitimate middle-of-the-order shortstop who steals bases on top.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The tension here is simple: 18.2% walk rate against a 32.5% strikeout rate, two numbers pulling hard in opposite directions from the same swing decisions. The contact is genuinely elite when it lands, 93.4 mph average exit velocity and an 18.0% barrel rate both sitting near the very top of the percentile distribution, which is why the xwOBA of .373 runs so far ahead of an xBA of .243. He makes loud, infrequent contact, walks at a rate that almost nobody matches, and the projection's .387 OBP follows directly from that combination. The whole profile hinges on whether that 32.5% strikeout rate plateaus or climbs, because if whiffs keep accumulating the batting average drags the floor down to a platoon-adjacent outcome, but if it stabilizes, 33 projected home runs with a .877 OPS looks like a first-division regular who gives Oakland something to actually build around.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The tension in Tatis's profile is the gap between how hard he hits the ball and what he does with it. A 53.4% hard-hit rate puts him in genuinely elite contact-quality company, and his 92.2 mph average exit velocity backs that up, yet a 28.3% whiff rate drags the translation down enough that the projection lands at .280/.355/.420 territory rather than the monster line the raw contact metrics tease. The bat-to-ball problem is specific: he's making hard contact when he connects, but he's not connecting often enough to fully cash those exit-velo receipts. If the whiff rate drifts toward his xBA-implied contact quality, the .420 SLG in the projection becomes a floor; if it doesn't, 16 projected home runs is roughly what you get from a guy who squares up the ball at that rate but misses too much. The 36 projected stolen bases are the quiet stabilizer here, the part of the profile that holds value even in the down-contact scenario.

reports.name: Michael Harris II
reports.published_report: The .293 xBA sits at the 96th percentile, and the .496 xSLG is in the 90th — the contact quality is genuinely elite, which is why the projection lands at 28 home runs and a .481 SLG despite a profile that should scare you at the plate. It should. A 44.9% chase rate and 3.8% walk rate are both near the bottom of the league, meaning Harris is essentially betting on his ability to do damage on pitches most hitters take or miss, and so far the Statcast contact numbers say he's winning that bet. The whole thing hinges on whether pitchers eventually bury him in the zone and he can't adjust, because if the chase rate stays that extreme and the hard contact dips even modestly, the .283 AVG and .313 OBP projection start looking optimistic fast. For now he's an everyday center fielder with above-average power output, elite defense, and a hit tool that outperforms his plate discipline in a way that's rare enough to take seriously.

reports.name: Josh Naylor
reports.published_report: The 28 projected stolen bases tell you more about how Statcast reads him than the 14 home runs do. Naylor makes contact at an elite rate, 12.3% strikeouts with an 18.1% whiff rate that ranks in the 83rd percentile, but the ball doesn't travel when he hits it, 87.7 mph average exit velocity and a 4.5% barrel rate that both sit near the bottom quarter of the league. His .273 xBA grades out well above his .319 xOWBA, which is the whole tension: he puts the ball in play often and in the right spots, but without the thump to make pitchers pay, he's dependent on a .264-.327-.381 slash staying healthy and the sprint speed (24.6 ft/s) not eroding further to squeeze value out of those grounders. A second-division regular who could slide toward a bench role if the contact profile softens.

The whole profile hinges on whether he keeps putting ball in play at a high clip, because a .318 xwOBA with a 40.5% chase rate and 6.0% walk rate leaves almost no margin for error if the hits stop falling. reports.name: Chase DeLauter
reports.published_report: The plate discipline numbers are what make this profile tick. DeLauter's 20.9% chase rate sits in the 95th percentile, and his 15.9% whiff rate pairs with a 14.1% strikeout rate that most hitters who hit the ball as hard as he does can't match. The 91.2 mph average exit velocity and 45.4% hard-hit rate say the contact quality is genuine, even if the 6.6% barrel rate keeps the ceiling from going sky-high — this is a line-drive-and-gap profile that earns its projected .278/.347/.446 through volume and discipline rather than loud power. He's slow, which limits him defensively and caps the upside, so the whole thing depends on whether that elite zone command holds as pitchers find angles on him. If it does, he's a useful everyday piece in Cleveland's lineup; if the discipline erodes, the lack of loud over-the-fence pop leaves a thin profile.

reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: That 38.1% chase rate is carrying the whole argument. Sánchez doesn't miss bats because hitters can't make contact, a 43.0% hard-hit rate and 89.3 mph average exit velocity say plenty of them do, he misses bats because hitters keep swinging at pitches they were never going to hit, and a 32.9% whiff rate confirms the damage when they do chase. The 5.5% walk rate tightens the profile further; he's not nibbling to generate that chase, he's locating well enough that the zone shapes the decision for him. If the chase rate regresses toward the field, the hard-hit exposure sitting quietly in the profile becomes the story instead of the footnote, and that 2.7 ERA projection gets harder to trust, but right now nothing in his Statcast profile suggests the discipline falls off.

reports.name: Luis Arraez
reports.published_report: A 4.5% strikeout rate is the whole skeleton of this profile, and everything else hangs off it. Arraez makes contact at a rate that almost doesn't exist anymore, which is why his xBA sits at .285 even though his average exit velocity of 87.0 mph ranks near the bottom of the league; he doesn't miss, so weak contact still becomes hits at a frequency that confounds the underlying power metrics. The tension is that his xwOBA and xSLG both land in the bottom third of qualified hitters, meaning the projection's .317 AVG is doing nearly all the work in getting him to a .785 OPS, and if his BABIP regresses to where his exit velocity says it should live, you're left with a low-OBP, no-power infielder rather than a useful fantasy piece. Believe in the bat-to-ball skill and the projection holds; stop believing, and it collapses fast.

The 88.0 mph average exit velocity ranks in the 30th percentile, so the projected 17 home runs aren't coming from raw thump — the 8.2% barrel rate is doing real work there, squeezing production out of contact quality that the overall exit velo profile doesn't quite support. reports.name: MacKenzie Gore
reports.published_report: The xERA says 3.82, the actual ERA projection says 4.46, and that gap is the whole profile in two numbers. Gore misses bats at a solid 26.0% clip but the barrel rate sits at 9.2%, and when contact lands, it lands hard. The walk rate at 8.4% means he can't strand trouble the way a cleaner pitcher does, and that command leakage keeps turning competent outings into four-run games before he escapes. If the walks come down and the barrel rate regresses toward the field, there's a mid-rotation arm here; if neither moves, 12 quality starts out of a full rotation's work is about what you're getting.

reports.name: Taj Bradley

reports.name: Emmet Sheehan
reports.published_report: The whiff and chase numbers are the whole argument here. Sheehan's 30.8% whiff rate and 35.0% chase rate both land in the 88th-89th percentile range, which means hitters are regularly expanding and missing, and yet the barrel rate sits at 10.5%, a bottom-of-the-chart figure that says when they do make contact, it's doing damage. That's the tension: elite bat-missing ability paired with a contact quality problem that the strikeout volume can only partially mask. The xERA of 3.96 says the true-talent floor is better than the projected 4.93 ERA suggests, but that gap closes only if he limits the barrels, and if that 10.5% persists in a bigger sample, the whiff gifts get spent.

If the contact quality somehow jumps, you get a fringe regular with speed utility; if it doesn't, what's left is a bench piece who can run and play multiple spots but won't hit enough to matter.

Boston is getting a catcher who can carry a lineup when he squares it up, and the barrel rate says that happens often enough to matter.

reports.name: Seiya Suzuki
reports.published_report: The gap between his plate discipline and his contact quality is the whole tension here. Suzuki chases at just 22.5%, a rate that puts him among the better two-way eyes in the league, and he draws walks at 11.8%, but his xBA sits at .247 and his average exit velocity of 88.9 mph is barely league-average — he earns counts he can't fully cash. A 9.9% barrel rate rescues the power profile enough that a projected .466 SLG and 26 home runs are credible, because he finds barrels even when he isn't squaring everything up. If the strikeout rate, currently 26.3%, climbs further as pitchers attack him in counts he can't punish, you get a walk-heavy .356 OBP carrying a flatter slugging line, a functional regular living off patience more than thump, but across 612 projected plate appearances the discipline and the barrels together point to a middle-of-the-order contributor whose floor is still useful even when the contact quality doesn't show up.

If the plate discipline translates, and the 13.2% walk rate at the MLB level is the most optimistic piece of the profile, he's a useful bench piece who gets on base and steals a bag; if the strikeout rate ticks up and the groundball-heavy contact that's inflating a .393 BABIP regresses, the whole argument collapses fast. Either an org-depth outfielder with a genuine walk-rate skill, or a guy whose counting stats look better than his ceiling ever will.

reports.name: Clayton Beeter
reports.published_report: Twenty saves projected out of Washington's bullpen is the number that earns a second look, and the fastball underpins all of it. At 95.6 mph with 2407 rpm of spin, Beeter's heater carries genuine swing-and-miss potential, the kind of combination that explains how a reliever on a rebuilding club ends up closing. The projection's 3.67 ERA and 1.3 WHIP across 52.0 innings suggest a functional backend arm, not a front-of-bullpen difference-maker, and that save total hinges almost entirely on Washington keeping him in the ninth-inning role rather than cycling through options as they typically do. If the spin plays the way the raw readings suggest it should, he's a viable streaming closer on a thin roster; if the Nationals redistribute save opportunities the way rebuilding teams often do, that 20 becomes noise fast.

reports.name: Will Sanders
reports.published_report: The profile is functional, not loud. If it doesn't, you've got an organizational piece who eats innings without getting hitters out.

reports.name: Isaac Lyon
reports.published_report: The walk rate is what makes this profile work, and what would unmake it. Across AA, A+, and A in 2026, Lyon is running a 2.8 BB/9 that translates to 3.2 at the MLB level, exactly matching the MLB average, which means the control edge he's leaning on right now is roughly a wash once the competition sharpens. The strikeout side is the honest problem: 8.4 K/9 in the minors becomes a 7.4 MLB-equivalent while the MLB average sits at 8.6, and without swing-and-miss to pair with the command, a 1.1 WHIP and 3.1 ERA across 84.3 innings looks more fragile than it reads. If the walk rate holds and the strikeouts nudge up as he faces better hitters, he's a back-end rotation piece; if the strikeouts stay where they are, what's left is a depth arm who has to be perfect to survive.

reports.name: Tekoah Roby
reports.published_report: The control is what makes this profile worth a second look. Across 47 innings at AA, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and when that command translates to an MLB context across AAA & AA, the walk rate holds — 2.7 BB/9, comfortably better than the MLB average, with a K-BB% that lands at 15.1%. The strikeout rate is the asterisk: his K/9 translates to 8.5, essentially matching what an average MLB arm produces, which means the profile lives or dies on whether the command stays elite enough to compensate. If it does, he's a useful depth piece who earns a rotation spot in a pinch; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats against better competition, he settles into a bullpen role where the control still plays.

reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.
